cast about.verb type: action — dynamic; searching is something you do, and it takes the progressive freely: *he was casting about for an excuse*.
cast about.passive: **no** — intransitive, and the prepositional passive fails too: ✗ *an excuse was cast about for*.

cast around.verb type: action — dynamic; the everyday American twin of *cast about*, equally at home in the progressive: *she was casting around for a chair*.
cast around.passive: **no** — intransitive; ✗ *a caterer was cast around for*.

cast aside.verb type: action — dynamic; a single act of rejection, not a state.
cast aside.passive: **yes**, and common in writing — *old loyalties were cast aside in a single afternoon*.

cast away.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses; in sense 2 (shipwreck) the verb survives almost only as a passive participle.
cast away.passive: **yes** — *he cast away his savings* → *his savings were cast away*; sense 2 is passive by default: *the crew were cast away on a reef*.

cast down.verb type: action — dynamic when you lower your eyes (sense 1); in sense 2 the participle sits close to an adjective of state — *she looked cast down*.
cast down.passive: **yes** — *her eyes were cast down*; sense 2 lives in the passive: *he was cast down by the second rejection*.

cast off.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: shedding something, leaving a dock, closing off stitches.
cast off.passive: **restricted** — fine where there is an object (*the old rules were cast off*, *the stitches are cast off loosely*), impossible in the boating sense, which has none: ✗ *was cast off by the crew* for *we cast off at dawn*.

cast on.verb type: action — dynamic; a knitting instruction, most often imperative.
cast on.passive: **restricted** — natural as a resulting state (*once forty stitches are cast on, join in the round*), odd with an agent: ✗ *eighty stitches were cast on by her*.

cast out.verb type: action — dynamic; a single act of expulsion.
cast out.passive: **yes**, and idiomatic — *she was cast out by her own congregation*.

catch at.verb type: action — dynamic; an attempt rather than a result, which is why the generic present works: *he catches at every rumor that suits him*.
catch at.passive: **no** in practice — the prepositional passive is not idiomatic: ✗ *my sleeve was caught at*, ✗ *the railing was caught at by her*.

catch on.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: sense 1 is a gradual change (*the name was catching on*), sense 2 a moment of understanding, not a state (*it took me three episodes to catch on*).
catch on.passive: **no** — intransitive; even with *to* there is no passive: ✗ *the trick was caught on to*.

catch out.verb type: action — dynamic; a single event of surprise or exposure.
catch out.passive: **yes** — and sense 1 is essentially passive-only in American use: *we were caught out by the storm halfway up the trail*.

catch up.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense; closing a gap takes time and takes the progressive: *I spent Sunday catching up*.
catch up.passive: **restricted** — nothing to passivize in the common intransitive senses (✗ *was caught up by me* for *I'll catch up*), but sense 4 exists only as a passive: *two of the clerks were caught up in the investigation*.

catch up on.verb type: action — dynamic; the work is done over a stretch of time: *she was catching up on six weeks of paperwork*.
catch up on.passive: **restricted** — the prepositional passive is possible but stiff (*the paperwork was finally caught up on*) and collapses with an agent: ✗ *sleep was caught up on by me*.

catch up with.verb type: action — dynamic; sense 2 personifies the trouble but is still an event: *the lies caught up with him in the end*.
catch up with.passive: **no** — ✗ *he was caught up with by the leaders*, ✗ *he was caught up with by his lies*. Keep it active.

choose up.verb type: action — dynamic; a one-time act of dividing a group into teams.
choose up.passive: **restricted** — *sides were chosen up before anyone thought to argue* passes, but an agent kills it: ✗ *sides were chosen up by the kids*.

cling on.verb type: action — dynamic but durative, an activity you keep doing: *she was clinging on with both hands*.
cling on.passive: **no** — intransitive; ✗ *the rail was clung on to*.

cling to.verb type: action — dynamic and durative in senses 1–2; sense 3 (a smell, a nickname) is closer to **stative**, a condition that simply lasts: *that nickname clung to him for thirty years*.
cling to.passive: **no** — the prepositional passive fails: ✗ *the raft was clung to*, ✗ *he was clung to by the nickname*.

come about.verb type: action — dynamic; an event verb of happening, with no agent behind it: *the merger came about almost by accident*.
come about.passive: **no** — intransitive, and like *happen* it will not passivize at all: ✗ *the merger was come about*.

come across.verb type: action — dynamic in sense 1, a chance discovery; in sense 2 *come across (as)* behaves as a **linking** verb, joining subject to a complement — *he comes across as arrogant*, *she came across very well*.
come across.passive: **no** — the standard example of a prepositional verb that refuses the passive: ✗ *an old photo was come across*. Say *was found* instead.

come after.verb type: action — dynamic; pursuit with hostile intent, fine in the progressive: *they're coming after you*.
come after.passive: **no** — ✗ *you will be come after by them*; *come* does not passivize under a preposition.

come along.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses — accompanying, progressing (*the garden is coming along nicely*), and turning up.
come along.passive: **no** — intransitive throughout; ✗ *the kids were come along*.

come apart.verb type: action — dynamic, a change of state with the thing itself as subject: *the binding came apart*, *he came apart on the stand*.
come apart.passive: **no** — intransitive, and the subject is already the affected thing, so a passive has nothing to promote: ✗ *the binding was come apart*.

come around.verb type: action — dynamic in all four senses; each is a change or an event, never a state.
come around.passive: **no** — intransitive; ✗ *her proposal was come around to*.

come at.verb type: action — dynamic in senses 1–2, an attack or an angle of approach; the fixed *come at a price* in sense 3 is **stative** — it means *cost*, not *move*.
come at.passive: **no** — ✗ *I was come at with a tire iron*; only the active works.

come away.verb type: action — dynamic: leaving with an impression (sense 1), or a part detaching itself (sense 2).
come away.passive: **no** — intransitive; ✗ *the handle was come away*, ✗ *the feeling was come away with*.

come back.verb type: action — dynamic in all four senses, including sense 3, where the memory is the subject: *the tune came back to her halfway through dinner*.
come back.passive: **no** — intransitive; ✗ *he was come back at by her*.

come between.verb type: action — dynamic, an event that damages a relationship, though the generic present reads almost stative: *nothing comes between that man and his Saturday*.
come between.passive: **no** — ✗ *the two brothers were come between by money*.

come by.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: a brief visit (sense 1) and an act of obtaining (sense 2).
come by.passive: **no** — ✗ *a key to the building was come by*. The fixed *hard to come by* is an infinitive, not a passive: *parts for that model are hard to come by*.

come down.verb type: action — dynamic; a fall in price, a handing-down, a collapse — all changes over time: *prices have come down about twenty percent*.
come down.passive: **no** — intransitive; ✗ *the old grandstand was come down*.

come down on.verb type: action — dynamic; a single act of punishment or criticism, often with *hard*.
come down on.passive: **no** — unlike *look down on*, this one will not passivize: ✗ *he was come down on hard by his editor*. Recast as active.

come down to.verb type: **stative** — it means *amount to*, not *move*, and resists the progressive: ✗ *it is coming down to money*.
come down to.passive: **no** — stative and unaccusative at once: ✗ *money is come down to by it*.

come down with.verb type: action — dynamic, a change of state you can be in the middle of: *I think I'm coming down with something*.
come down with.passive: **no** — ✗ *strep was come down with by half the class*.

come forward.verb type: action — dynamic; a voluntary act, normally reported as a single event.
come forward.passive: **no** — intransitive; ✗ *the emails were come forward with*.

come from.verb type: **stative** in senses 1–2 — origin, not motion, and it stays in the simple present even of someone long dead: *he comes from a family of teachers*, ✗ *he is coming from Ohio* in that sense. A live source allows the progressive: *that smell is coming from under the sink*.
come from.passive: **no** — stative and prepositional both: ✗ *Ohio is come from by her grandparents*.

come in.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense — arriving, finishing a race, becoming fashionable: *not much is coming in this quarter*.
come in.passive: **no** — intransitive; and *come in handy* takes an adjective, not an object: ✗ *it was come in handy*.

come in for.verb type: action — dynamic, an event of receiving something aimed at you (*the mayor came in for heavy criticism*); the progressive is fine: *the plan is coming in for criticism from both sides*.
come in for.passive: **no.** The object is a fixed idiomatic noun (*criticism, blame, scrutiny, praise*) that cannot be promoted: ✗ *heavy criticism was come in for by the mayor*. The phrase is already the receiving end — for a passive, switch verbs: *the mayor was criticized*.

come into.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, the sudden acquiring (*he came into a little money*) and the entering of a state (*the rules come into effect on the first*). Progressive fine: *the new fee is coming into effect next month*.
come into.passive: **no.** A prepositional verb whose object never moves to subject: ✗ *a little money was come into by him*, ✗ *effect was come into by the rules*. Say *he inherited the money* / *the rules took effect*.

come off.verb type: action — dynamic in the detaching (*the knob came off*), succeeding (*the party almost didn't come off*), and fresh-from senses (*they're coming off three straight wins*). *Come off as* is **linking (copular)**: what follows describes the subject, not an object — *he comes off as colder than he is*.
come off.passive: **no.** Senses 1–2 are intransitive, so there is nothing to promote: ✗ *the stain was come off*. The prepositional uses refuse it too: ✗ *the bench was come off*, ✗ *three straight wins are being come off*.

come on.verb type: action — dynamic throughout: a light or a heater starting (*the porch light comes on at dusk*), an illness or weather beginning (*I feel a headache coming on*), an actor entering (*she comes on after the intermission*). *Come on!* is a fixed interjection with no tense or aspect of its own.
come on.passive: **no** — intransitive in every sense, so no passive exists: ✗ *the heat was come on*, ✗ *the stage was come on by her*.

come on to.verb type: action — dynamic; a deliberate act, and the progressive is normal: *he swears he wasn't coming on to anyone*.
come on to.passive: **yes** — one of the few *come* phrasals that passivizes cleanly, because the object is a person: *nobody wants to be come on to by a manager*, *she'd been come on to twice that night*.

come out.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense: being released (*the book comes out in March*), becoming known (*the truth came out*), being removed (*red wine won't come out of linen*), coming out publicly (*he came out at nineteen*). Sense 5 shades into **linking**, with an adjective describing the subject: *none of the pictures came out well*.
come out.passive: **no** — intransitive throughout; what is revealed or released is already the subject: ✗ *the truth was come out*, ✗ *the book has been come out in March*. Use *be published*, *be revealed*.

come out with.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, the blurting (*then he came out with the strangest question*) and the releasing (*they come out with a new version every fall*); progressive fine: *they're coming out with a cheaper model*.
come out with.passive: **no** in practice. The three-part passive is unusable here: ✗ *a cheaper model has been come out with*, ✗ *the whole story was come out with*. Switch verbs: *a cheaper model has been released*.

come over.verb type: action — dynamic in the visiting sense (*her parents came over for coffee*) and in the seizing-feeling sense (*a wave of dizziness came over him*). The British *come over as* is **linking**: *in print he comes over as rather severe*.
come over.passive: **no.** Sense 1 is intransitive (✗ *my house was come over*), and the feeling sense refuses promotion even though a person follows: ✗ *he was come over by a wave of dizziness*, ✗ *I was come over by something*.

come round.verb type: action — dynamic in all four senses: regaining consciousness (*she came round ten minutes later*), being won over (*he'll come round to the idea*), dropping by, and recurring (*exam season comes round faster every year*).
come round.passive: **no** — intransitive, so there is no passive at all: ✗ *she was come round after the anesthetic*, ✗ *the idea was come round to*.

come through.verb type: action — dynamic: delivering (*he came through with the money*), surviving (*he came through the surgery fine*), and paperwork being approved (*the visa finally came through*). Progressive fine: *if the transfer is coming through today, we can close*.
come through.passive: **no.** Sense 1 and sense 3 are intransitive (✗ *the money was come through with*), and the survive sense resists the prepositional passive: ✗ *the surgery was come through*, ✗ *the fire was come through by the family*.

come to.verb type: **Both.** Sense 1 is action — dynamic and intransitive: *he came to on the kitchen floor*. Sense 2 (amount to) is **stative**, like *cost*, and rejects the progressive: ✗ *the bill is coming to forty-two dollars*. Senses 3–4 are dynamic again: *I hope it doesn't come to a lawsuit*, *the name came to me in the shower*.
come to.passive: **no.** Sense 1 has no object at all. The stative amount sense refuses the passive the way *cost* does: ✗ *forty-two dollars was come to by the bill*; so does the occur-to sense: ✗ *I was come to by the name*.

come together.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, people assembling (*the town came together after the flood*) and a plan taking shape (*the album came together in about three weeks*); progressive normal: *it's finally coming together*.
come together.passive: **no** — intransitive; the people or the parts are the subject already: ✗ *the town was come together*, ✗ *the album has been come together*.

come under.verb type: **Both.** Sense 1 (fall within a category or jurisdiction) is **stative** — a standing relationship, awkward in the progressive: ✗ *that department is coming under the state*. Sense 2 is action — dynamic: *the proposal came under fire from both parties*.
come under.passive: **no.** A prepositional verb whose object is a fixed noun that cannot be promoted: ✗ *fire was come under by the proposal*, ✗ *a different ordinance is come under by short rentals*. For the passive idea use *was criticized*, *was reviewed*.

come up.verb type: action — dynamic in all four senses: a topic arising (*her name came up twice*), approaching someone (*a stranger came up to me*), an event nearing (*finals are coming up fast*), and rising (*the sun came up*).
come up.passive: **no** — intransitive; the topic or the sun is the subject, never an object: ✗ *her name was come up*, ✗ *I was come up to by a stranger*.

come up against.verb type: action — dynamic; an event of meeting resistance, and the progressive is fine: *we're coming up against the same permit problem again*.
come up against.passive: **no** in practice — the three-part passive is not used: ✗ *the same permit problem was come up against twice*, ✗ *opposition was come up against by the bill*. Rephrase with *meet* or *run into*.

come up with.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, producing an idea (*she came up with the name in four seconds*) and producing money (*they had to come up with six thousand by Friday*); progressive normal: *he's coming up with excuses*.
come up with.passive: **restricted.** Possible but clumsy, and only with a light subject and no *by*-phrase: *no better explanation was ever come up with*. Avoid it with an agent — ✗ *the name was come up with by her* — and never in the money sense: ✗ *six thousand had to be come up with*.

come upon.verb type: action — dynamic: a chance discovery (*she came upon the letters in the attic*) or, in literary use, a feeling or a season overtaking someone (*a great weariness came upon him*). Not progressive-friendly in the discovery sense, since the event is instantaneous.
come upon.passive: **restricted**, and rare enough to avoid. The literary discovery sense is occasionally passivized (*the cache was come upon by hikers*), but ✗ *the letters were come upon by her* is poor, and the feeling sense refuses it outright: ✗ *he was come upon by a great weariness*.

cost out.verb type: action — dynamic; a piece of work carried out on a budget, with the progressive fine: *finance is costing out both options this week*. Note the regular past in this sense — *we costed it out* — unlike plain stative *cost*, which never changes and rejects the progressive.
cost out.passive: **yes**, and common in business writing: *the maintenance has never been costed out*, *the whole program was costed out at nine million*.

creep in.verb type: action — dynamic, a slow unnoticed arrival: *small errors creep in whenever the data is retyped*, *a note of impatience crept in toward the end*. Progressive fine: *doubt was creeping in*.
creep in.passive: **no** — intransitive; the errors or the doubt are the subject: ✗ *errors are crept in*. The *into* variant resists the prepositional passive too: ✗ *every edition is crept into by typos*.

creep out.verb type: **Both.** Sense 1 is action — dynamic and causative, a thing producing a feeling in someone: *that street creeps me out after dark*. Sense 2 is action — dynamic and intransitive: *he crept out at four in the morning*. Note the split past: regular *creeped* in sense 1, irregular *crept* in sense 2.
creep out.passive: **yes** in the unnerve sense, and very common: *I was completely creeped out by the doll*, *half the theater got creeped out by the soundtrack*. **No** passive of the slip-away sense — it has no object: ✗ *the side door was crept out*.

creep up.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, approaching quietly (*don't creep up behind me*) and rising by small amounts (*rents have crept up every year*); progressive fine: *costs were creeping up all winter*.
creep up.passive: **no** — intransitive in both senses: ✗ *I was crept up behind*, ✗ *the estimate is crept up*.

creep up on.verb type: action — dynamic; a stealthy approach, literal or figurative, and the progressive is normal: *the deadline is creeping up on us again*.
creep up on.passive: **restricted.** Natural with a personal subject and no agent, especially in the *-ing* form: *nobody likes being crept up on in a parking garage*. It gets clumsy with a *by*-phrase — ✗ *the bird was crept up on by the cat* — and the time sense refuses it: ✗ *we have been crept up on by the deadline*.

cut across.verb type: **Both.** Sense 1 is action — dynamic: *we cut across the field instead of following the road*. Sense 2 (run through ordinary divisions) is **stative**, a standing property rather than an event, and sits badly in the progressive: ✗ *grief is cutting across everything else*.
cut across.passive: **no.** ✗ *the field was cut across* means something else entirely (a cut made in it), and the figurative sense refuses promotion: ✗ *party lines were cut across by the measure*, ✗ *every department was cut across by the complaints*.

cut away.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, removing material (*cut away the dead growth*) and switching shots (*the director cuts away to the crowd*); progressive fine in both: *they're cutting away to a commercial*.
cut away.passive: **yes** in sense 1, and it is the usual form in surgical and repair writing: *the scar tissue was cut away first*, *once the rot has been cut away you can see the damage*. **No** passive of the film sense, which has no object: ✗ *the crowd was cut away to*.

cut back.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, reducing (*we had to cut back after the second kid*) and pruning (*cut back the hydrangeas in March*); progressive fine: *the plant is cutting back to four days a week*.
cut back.passive: **yes** in the pruning sense: *the raspberries were cut back almost to the ground*. **No** passive of the reduce sense, which takes no object — ✗ *the plant was cut back to four days* would be read as pruning; say *production was cut* or *hours were reduced*.

cut back on.verb type: action — dynamic; a deliberate reduction, and the progressive is normal: *she's been cutting back on shifts since the baby*.
cut back on.passive: **restricted** — possible but stiff, and only without an agent: *overtime was cut back on rather than cut altogether*. Avoid it with *by*: ✗ *salt was cut back on by him*. Plain *was reduced* is the natural passive.

cut down.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: felling (*they cut down the elm*), reducing (*cut the introduction down to a page*), and the literary killing sense (*the fever cut him down at thirty-one*). Progressive fine: *I'm cutting down to one cup a day*.
cut down.passive: **yes**, and in sense 3 the passive is the usual form: *a whole generation was cut down in four years*. Also *the elm was cut down last spring*, *the introduction has been cut down to a page*. No passive of the intransitive *I've cut down to one cup a day*.

cut down on.verb type: action — dynamic; a gradual reduction of consumption or activity, comfortable in the progressive: *I'm trying to cut down on screen time*.
cut down on.passive: **restricted** — grammatical but awkward, and only agentless: *screen time has been cut down on all year*. ✗ *red meat was cut down on by her* is bad; native writers use *was reduced* or *she cut down on it*.

cut in.verb type: action — dynamic in all four senses: interrupting (*she cut in before he could finish*), pulling in front (*a pickup cut in*), giving a share (*they cut him in for ten percent*), and a motor starting by itself (*the compressor cut in*).
cut in.passive: **restricted** — **yes** only in the share sense, where it is idiomatic: *he was cut in for ten percent*, *the two engineers were cut in for a point each*. **No** passive of the other three, which take no object: ✗ *the conversation was cut in*, ✗ *the generator is cut in within four seconds*.

cut into.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: eroding (*the new fees cut into our margin*), slicing (*the rope cut into his palms*), and interrupting (*he cut into the argument with a question*); progressive fine: *practice is cutting into every weekday evening*.
cut into.passive: **no** in practice. The prepositional passive is marginal at best — ✗ *our margin was cut into by the new fees*, ✗ *his palms were cut into by the rope* — and the interrupt sense refuses it outright: ✗ *the argument was cut into*. Say *the fees ate into our margin* or *our margin shrank*.

cut loose.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, freeing or severing (*he cut the trailer loose*) and letting yourself go (*at a wedding he cuts loose*). *Loose* here is a resultative adjective describing the object, not an ordinary particle — compare *cut it free*.
cut loose.passive: **yes** in the transitive sense, and it is common of people: *she was cut loose after one album*, *the trailer had been cut loose miles back*. **No** passive of the enjoy-yourself sense, which has no object: ✗ *the kitchen staff was cut loose* would mean they were fired.

cut off.verb type: action — dynamic in all six senses: severing (*cut off the stems at an angle*), disconnecting a service, isolating, interrupting (*she cut him off mid-sentence*), pulling in front of a driver, and disinheriting (*his father cut him off*).
cut off.passive: **yes**, in every sense, and in sense 3 the passive is the normal form: *the valley was cut off for six days*, *the electricity was cut off on a Friday*, *he was cut off without a cent*, *I got cut off on the ramp*.

cut out.verb type: action — dynamic: removing by cutting (*she cut out the pattern*), stopping (*cut it out*), an engine quitting (*the outboard cut out*), excluding (*they cut them out of the deal*). Sense 5, *be cut out for*, is a fixed **stative** adjectival passive — a standing fitness, not an event: *he wasn't cut out for sales*.
cut out.passive: **yes** in senses 1–2 and 4: *the article was cut out and mailed to me*, *soda has been cut out entirely*, *they were cut out of the deal*. Sense 5 exists **only** in the passive, with no active counterpart: ✗ *sales didn't cut him out for*. **No** passive of the engine sense: ✗ *the outboard was cut out*.

cut through.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, taking a shortcut (*we cut through the alley*) and getting past an obstruction (*her one question cut through an hour of hedging*); progressive fine: *the siren was cutting through the noise*.
cut through.passive: **no.** ✗ *the alley was cut through* is read as a hole being made in it, not a shortcut, and the figurative sense is barely better: ✗ *the red tape was cut through by somebody*. Use an active subject, or switch to *get past* / *break through*.

cut up.verb type: action — dynamic in the first two senses, dividing (*cut up the onions*) and clowning around (*he cuts up the second a camera appears*). Sense 3, the British *be cut up*, is a **stative** adjectival passive describing a state of distress: *she was terribly cut up about the dog*.
cut up.passive: **yes** in sense 1: *the potatoes were washed and cut up*, *the cardboard had been cut up small enough for the bin*. **No** passive of the clown-around sense, which has no object: ✗ *the class was cut up in*. Sense 3 is passive in form only — it has no active: ✗ *the dog cut her up*.
